# IAC downgrades

These descriptions are generated from the Tuning package of FCScore and describe what FCScore measures for each downgrade. See the [downgrade reference](index.md) for how to read them.

Generated from Tuning commit: `9bb5210`.

**Rulebook source**

> - [IAC Contest Rules 2026, Revision C](https://www.iac.org/system/files/IAC%20Rule%20Book%202026%20Rev%20C.pdf)
>
> This configuration is for powered aircraft.
>
> The judging references in `judging_guide.json` are verbatim extracts from the IAC rules, identified by their rule number: Chapter 26 (Grading of Figures), Chapter 27 (Basic Criteria for Judging Aerobatic Figures), Chapter 28 (Family-Specific Grading Criteria), and the box and altitude rules in Chapters 7 and 13. The box limits are contest penalties in the rules rather than figure deductions, so the FCScore box downgrades are estimates of their severity.
>
> The CIVA rules (FAI Sporting Code Section 6 Part 1) are related to the IAC rules but not identical, so they should be added as a separate set of references rather than assumed to match.

Rulebook extracts are quoted verbatim and listed under [Rulebook references](#rulebook-references).

## Intra-element downgrades

### Horizontal Line Climb {#climb}

`climb`

Checks that horizontal lines are flown at constant altitude, with no climb or descent in the flight path. Only growth in the climb or descent angle is charged, so returning to level flight is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    Horizontal lines must be flown at a constant altitude and are judged on the flight path rather than the attitude, because the attitude needed for level flight varies with aircraft type and airspeed. The line should look level whatever angle the nose is held at.

    FCScore measures the angle between the aircraft's flight path and the horizontal over each horizontal line and charges each increase in the absolute angle; a decrease is free. A climb or descent already present when the line starts was charged on the element that created it, so it is not charged again. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule. The line between two figures belongs to the next figure, so what is measured on the exit line of a figure is reported with the following figure, and the figure's own score keeps the rest.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Horizontal lines are to be flown at a constant altitude and judged on flight path, not attitude.
>
> [27.5.1](#rb-lines.horizontal)

> Deduct 0.5 points for every 2.5 degrees of angular error or fraction thereof.
>
> [27.6.1](#rb-general.angle_rule)

### Horizontal Line Heading {#heading}

`heading`

Checks that the nose stays parallel to the box axis on horizontal lines. Only growth in the heading error is charged, so swinging back is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    On horizontal lines the aircraft's heading must remain parallel to the X or Y axis of the box. A pilot may correct for wind drift, but if the correction is visible to the judge the standard deduction of one point per 5° of heading deviation applies.

    FCScore measures the angle of the fuselage, not the flight path, relative to the template heading in the horizontal plane, and charges each increase in the absolute angle over the line; a decrease is free. Because the nose direction is measured, a visible crab against a crosswind shows up here, but only the part that builds up during the line is charged. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule. The line between two figures belongs to the next figure, so what is measured on the exit line of a figure is reported with the following figure, and the figure's own score keeps the rest.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The aircraft’s heading must remain parallel to the X or Y axis.
>
> [27.5.2](#rb-lines.heading)

> Competitors may attempt to correct for wind drift but if these corrections are visible to the judge the standard deduction of one (1) point per five (5) degrees of heading deviation must be given.
>
> [27.14.1](#rb-general.wind_correction)

### Vertical/45° Line Yaw {#yaw}

`yaw`

Checks that the nose does not swing sideways on vertical and 45° lines. Only growth in the sideways attitude error is charged, so swinging back is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    Vertical and 45° lines are judged on the attitude of the aircraft, according to its zero-lift axis, not on the flight path, so wind drift is ignored but the aircraft must point exactly along the line. The wings must also stay aligned with a box axis and the horizon.

    FCScore measures the angle of the fuselage relative to the template line in the sideways (yaw) direction and charges each increase in the absolute angle over the line; a decrease is free. It uses the fuselage centre-line as the reference rather than your zero-lift axis, which it does not know. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Vertical lines are judged on the attitude of the aircraft, according to its zero-lift axis, and not the flight path.
>
> [27.3.1](#rb-lines.vertical)

> 45 Degree lines are judged according to the perfect vertical attitude plus or minus 45 degrees.
>
> [27.4.1](#rb-lines.diagonal)

### Turn Altitude Change {#axial_track}

`axial_track`

Checks that turns hold a constant altitude. Only growth in the climb or descent angle of the flight path around the turn is charged, so returning to level flight is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    In turns and rolling turns the altitude must be constant: a change costs one point for every 5° or 100 feet. Wind effects on a turn are not downgraded, but the pilot must still hold the turn level.

    FCScore measures the angle between the flight path and the horizontal plane of the turn, and charges each increase in the absolute angle; a decrease is free. It applies to horizontal arcs such as turns and rolling turns, and not to loops in a vertical plane. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The altitude must be constant. If the altitude changes, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees or 100 feet.
>
> [28.4.5](#rb-turns.altitude)

### Loop Plane Attitude {#axial_attitude}

`axial_attitude`

Checks that the nose stays in the plane of the loop. Only growth in the out-of-plane angle of the fuselage is charged, so swinging back is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    A looping line is a vertically curving path that must have a constant radius. IAC has no rule specific to the nose direction in a loop, so the general rule applies: one point for every 5° of angular error.

    FCScore measures the angle of the fuselage out of the plane of the loop and charges each increase in the absolute angle; a decrease is free. It measures the direction the nose points, so a crab angle held against a crosswind shows up here, even though the rules give no deduction for the loop's finish being displaced sideways by crosswind. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

### Loop Exit Flight Path {#radial_track}

`radial_track`

Checks that the flight path is exactly level when a loop returns to horizontal flight. The full angle error at the end of the loop is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    When a looping line returns to a horizontal line, that line is judged on flight path, so the loop must finish with the flight path exactly horizontal, with no extra or missing degrees of arc.

    FCScore takes the last point of the loop and charges the whole angle between the flight path and the template within the plane of the loop. It is an absolute measure at the end of the loop, so an over- or under-flown arc is charged here once and the line that follows is only charged for further change. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Horizontal lines are to be flown at a constant altitude and judged on flight path, not attitude.

### Roll Angle on Lines {#line_roll}

`line_roll`

Checks that the wings stay aligned on lines without a roll, and that there is no rolling during a stall turn or tailslide. Only growth in the roll angle error is charged, so levelling the wings again is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    On vertical lines the wings must be aligned with a box axis and the horizon, and during a stall turn pivot there must be no rolling or pitching motion, at one point per 5°. A tailslide is judged in the same way.

    FCScore measures the roll angle relative to the template on lines that contain no roll, and through stall turns and tailslides, and charges each increase in the absolute roll error; a decrease is free. An angle already present at the start of the element is not charged again, as it was charged where it arose. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule. The line between two figures belongs to the next figure, so what is measured on the exit line of a figure is reported with the following figure, and the figure's own score keeps the rest.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The wings must be aligned with a box axis and the horizon.
>
> [27.3.2](#rb-lines.vertical_wings)

> If there is any rolling or pitching motion during the pivot, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees.
>
> [28.8.4](#rb-stall_turns.pivot_motion)

### Roll Angle in Rolling Turn Pauses {#circle_pause_roll}

`circle_pause_roll`

Checks that the wings stay at the template attitude during a brief pause between the rolls of a rolling turn. Only growth in the roll angle error is charged, so returning to the attitude is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    A rolling turn may pause briefly where the roll direction changes. The IAC rules downgrade rolling turns only for changes to the rate of roll, the rate of turn and altitude; the judge may expect the aircraft to be upright or inverted at these points, but there is no specific deduction for its attitude there. This downgrade is an FCScore approximation that applies the general angle rule, one point for every 5° of error.

    FCScore measures the roll angle relative to the template on the short level loop segments that sit between two rolling segments of a turn, and charges each increase in the absolute roll error; a decrease is free. An angle already present at the start of the pause is not charged again. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Deduct 0.5 points for every 2.5 degrees of angular error or fraction thereof.
>
> [27.6.1](#rb-general.angle_rule)

### Bank Angle in Turns {#turn_roll}

`turn_roll`

Checks that the bank angle established for a turn is held. Only growth in the bank angle error during the turn is charged, so returning to the bank is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    Once the bank angle of a turn has been established it must not change: any change costs one point for every 5°. The bank must be at least 60° when the heading change begins.

    FCScore measures how the bank angle differs from the angle established at the start of the turn, taking an established bank below 60° or above 90° as 60° or 90°, and charges each increase in the absolute error; a decrease is free. It applies to turns that contain no roll. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> If there is any change to the established angle of bank, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees.
>
> [28.5.3](#rb-turns.bank)

### Roll Rotation Amount {#roll_roll}

`roll_roll`

Checks that a roll, snap or spin finishes at the planned attitude. At the point of maximum rotation, the roll attitude is compared with the planned attitude and the difference is charged once, so both over- and under-rotation count. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    A roll must end with a precise stop, with the wings at the desired degree of rotation, and over- or under-rotation costs one point for every 5°. A snap or spin must also end at its prescribed rotation.

    FCScore finds the point of maximum rotation in each roll, snap or spin and compares the aircraft's roll attitude there with the planned attitude. It assesses the final attitude, not the total number of degrees rolled, although it tracks the rotation continuously (allowing for the angle wrapping round at 180°) so that a roll that overshoots by a full turn is not mistaken for a correct one. Over-rotation and under-rotation are charged equally, as a single absolute error at that point. Rolling back afterwards is charged separately, and the over-rotation is not charged a second time when the pilot corrects it. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> The rotation must end with a precise stop with the wings at the desired degree of rotation. If there is any over or under rotation, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees.
>
> [28.20.2](#rb-rolls.stop)

> Downgrades are always made for the original error but not for any corrections which immediately follow.
>
> [26.6.2](#rb-general.corrections)

### Turn Entry Bank Angle {#preturn_roll}

`preturn_roll`

Checks that the roll into a turn establishes at least 60° of bank. Any shortfall below 60° at the end of the roll is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    A competition turn starts by establishing a bank of at least 60° while maintaining the initial heading, before the heading change begins.

    FCScore takes the point of maximum rotation of the roll that precedes a turn, measures the bank angle from wings level, and charges any amount by which it is below 60°. A bank of more than 60° is not charged here. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

### Roll Rebound {#rebound}

`rebound`

Checks that a roll stays where it stopped. After the maximum rotation, any growth in the roll error, such as bouncing back past the target or wobbling, is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    The rotation must end with a precise stop at the desired angle. The rules charge an over-rotation once and do not charge again for rolling the wings back to the correct geometry.

    FCScore looks at each rotating element after the point of maximum rotation and charges each increase in the absolute roll error. An over-rotation is charged once, at the point of maximum rotation, so rolling back from it is not charged again, but rolling back past the target or rocking the wings creates a new increase that is charged. A decrease in the error is free. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Downgrades are always made for the original error but not for any corrections which immediately follow.
>
> [26.6.2](#rb-general.corrections)

> The rotation must end with a precise stop with the wings at the desired degree of rotation. If there is any over or under rotation, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees.
>
> [28.20.2](#rb-rolls.stop)

### Roll Centring on the Loop {#loop_roll_centre}

`loop_roll_centre`

Checks that a roll, or roll combination, on a loop is centred on the apex or nadir. The angle between the middle of the rolling section and the apex is charged once for the whole section. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: loops viewed edge-on, and loops high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    Rolls may appear on looping lines. The rolls must be centered symmetrically about the apex or nadir and be integrated into the radius. The pilot chooses how much of the loop the roll or roll combination uses, but it must take the same amount of loop before the apex as after it. IAC has no standard deduction for a roll that is off centre, so the general rule applies: one point for every 5° of error.

    FCScore takes the whole rolling section of one loop as a single window: the rolls and snaps and the pauses between them, but not the loop flown either side of it. It reads the flight path elevation where the section starts and where it ends. The path falls through the top of a loop and rises through the bottom, so the average of the two elevations is zero when the section is centred about the apex or nadir, whatever the size and shape of the loop (round, P, Q or reversing) and however much of it the pilot uses. An error of 10° in where the roll sits on the loop is a 10° error in that average. FCScore charges its size once, at the end of the section, as an angle, so a roll centred early and one centred late cost the same. It is measured from the flown path, so a roll that misses the apex altogether is still charged for how far from it it was. Rolls and snaps on straight lines are not covered, and neither are loops whose roll fills the whole loop element, which have no apex to centre on. The extra deduction for flying part of a roll on a straight line is not measured here. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Where a roll sits on a loop is easiest to judge when the loop is viewed face-on (the judge looking along the loop's axis) and hardest when it is seen edge-on, where the position along the loop is hidden. It is also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side. The weighting does not depend on how much of the loop the roll uses. Large errors are counted in full.

> Rolls may appear on Looping Lines. The rolls must be centered symmetrically about the apex or nadir and be integrated into the radius. … If any part of the roll or roll combination is flown on a straight line, deduct at least two (2) points.
>
> [27.12.1-27.12.2](#rb-loops.integrated_rolls)

### Snap Centring on the Loop {#loop_snap_centre}

`loop_snap_centre`

Checks that a snap roll on a loop is centred on the apex or nadir. The angle between the middle of the rolling section and the apex is charged once for the whole section. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: loops viewed edge-on, and loops high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    A snap roll on a loop is part of the same rolling section as the rolls on that loop, and the whole section must be centred about the apex or nadir. The snap is not scored separately: FCScore scores the rolls, snaps and pauses of the loop together as one window, under the roll centring downgrade (loop_roll_centre), and this key is only used to join the snap into it. A loop whose only roll is a snap is scored in the same way, with the snap centred on the apex.

    FCScore takes the whole rolling section of one loop as a single window: the rolls and snaps and the pauses between them, but not the loop flown either side of it. It reads the flight path elevation where the section starts and where it ends. The path falls through the top of a loop and rises through the bottom, so the average of the two elevations is zero when the section is centred about the apex or nadir, whatever the size and shape of the loop (round, P, Q or reversing) and however much of it the pilot uses. An error of 10° in where the roll sits on the loop is a 10° error in that average. FCScore charges its size once, at the end of the section, as an angle, so a roll centred early and one centred late cost the same. It is measured from the flown path, so a roll that misses the apex altogether is still charged for how far from it it was. Rolls and snaps on straight lines are not covered, and neither are loops whose roll fills the whole loop element, which have no apex to centre on. The extra deduction for flying part of a roll on a straight line is not measured here. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Where a roll sits on a loop is easiest to judge when the loop is viewed face-on (the judge looking along the loop's axis) and hardest when it is seen edge-on, where the position along the loop is hidden. It is also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side. The weighting does not depend on how much of the loop the roll uses. Large errors are counted in full.

> Rolls may appear on Looping Lines. The rolls must be centered symmetrically about the apex or nadir and be integrated into the radius. … If any part of the roll or roll combination is flown on a straight line, deduct at least two (2) points.
>
> [27.12.1-27.12.2](#rb-loops.integrated_rolls)

### Pause Centring on the Loop {#loop_pause_centre}

`loop_pause_centre`

Checks that a pause between rolls on a loop is centred on the apex or nadir. The angle between the middle of the rolling section and the apex is charged once for the whole section. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: loops viewed edge-on, and loops high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    A pause between two rolls or snaps on a loop is part of the same rolling section as the rolls on that loop, and the whole section must be centred about the apex or nadir. The pause is not scored separately: FCScore scores the rolls, snaps and pauses of the loop together as one window, under the roll centring downgrade (loop_roll_centre), and this key is only used to join the pause into it. The pads of the loop before and after the rolling section are not part of it.

    FCScore takes the whole rolling section of one loop as a single window: the rolls and snaps and the pauses between them, but not the loop flown either side of it. It reads the flight path elevation where the section starts and where it ends. The path falls through the top of a loop and rises through the bottom, so the average of the two elevations is zero when the section is centred about the apex or nadir, whatever the size and shape of the loop (round, P, Q or reversing) and however much of it the pilot uses. An error of 10° in where the roll sits on the loop is a 10° error in that average. FCScore charges its size once, at the end of the section, as an angle, so a roll centred early and one centred late cost the same. It is measured from the flown path, so a roll that misses the apex altogether is still charged for how far from it it was. Rolls and snaps on straight lines are not covered, and neither are loops whose roll fills the whole loop element, which have no apex to centre on. The extra deduction for flying part of a roll on a straight line is not measured here. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Where a roll sits on a loop is easiest to judge when the loop is viewed face-on (the judge looking along the loop's axis) and hardest when it is seen edge-on, where the position along the loop is hidden. It is also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side. The weighting does not depend on how much of the loop the roll uses. Large errors are counted in full.

> Rolls may appear on Looping Lines. The rolls must be centered symmetrically about the apex or nadir and be integrated into the radius. … If any part of the roll or roll combination is flown on a straight line, deduct at least two (2) points.
>
> [27.12.1-27.12.2](#rb-loops.integrated_rolls)

### Roll Rate Consistency {#roll_rate}

`roll_rate`

Checks that the roll rate is constant through each roll. The size of the variation in roll rate, compared with the average, is charged once for the roll. Small variations are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, and for short part-rolls that give less to judge.

??? note "Details"

    Rolls must be flown at a constant roll rate: any variance costs one point, for example slowing sharply for the last 45° of a 180° roll. Rolling turns are judged in the same way.

    FCScore measures the roll rate throughout each roll and calculates how much it varies as a fraction of its average. A steady roll scores zero, whatever its rate. The more the rate varies, the larger the downgrade. FCScore charges in proportion to the variation, not in whole points per occurrence.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll rate is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than when you are looking at its top or underside, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. The weighting also grows with the amount of roll flown: a full roll or more counts fully, a half roll counts about half, because short rolls give the judge less to assess. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors.

> Slow Rolls must be flown at a constant roll rate. If there is any variance in the roll rate, deduct one (1) point per variation.
>
> [28.20.1](#rb-rolls.rate)

> There must be a constant rate of roll. Deduct for each variation.
>
> [28.6.5](#rb-turns.rolling_rate)

### Roll Pauses {#roll_excitation}

`roll_excitation`

Checks that the roll does not stop partway. The share of the roll for which the roll rate is close to zero, or reversed, is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see (aircraft viewed from above or below, or high or wide in the box) and short rotations count for less.

??? note "Details"

    The rate of roll must not stop in a slow roll or a rolling turn, apart from a brief pause when changing roll direction, and each stop is deducted.

    FCScore counts the time during each roll in which the roll rate is effectively zero or reversed. A rate below about 1.5° per second counts as fully stopped, a rate above about 3° per second counts as moving, and values in between count partly. The downgrade is based on the fraction of the roll's duration spent stopped, so a long hold costs more than a brief one.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. A stop in the rotation is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than from above or below, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. The weighting is also scaled by the amount of rotation flown, so a short rotation counts for less than a full one.

> Slow Rolls must be flown at a constant roll rate. If there is any variance in the roll rate, deduct one (1) point per variation.
>
> [28.20.1](#rb-rolls.rate)

> The rate of roll must not stop (aside from any brief pause when changing roll directions). Deduct for each stop.
>
> [28.6.6](#rb-turns.rolling_stop)

### Loop Roundness {#radius}

`radius`

Checks that each loop is round, with a constant radius throughout. The variation of the radius within the loop, compared with its average, is charged once for the loop. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: loops viewed edge-on, high or wide in the box, and part-loops that show less of the shape.

??? note "Details"

    Looping lines must have a constant radius. IAC has no standard deduction for changes in radius, and leaves judges to use a consistent method, for example a point for each visible variation and two for a major deviation.

    FCScore fits a circle to the flown path of the loop in the plane of the loop and measures how much the aircraft's distance from the fitted centre varies, as a fraction of the average radius. A perfectly round loop scores zero, whatever its size, and the more the radius varies the larger the downgrade.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Shape errors are easiest to see when the loop is viewed face-on (the judge looking along the loop's axis) and hardest when it is seen edge-on, where distortions are hidden. They are also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side, and the weighting is scaled by how much of a full loop is flown: a complete loop counts fully, a quarter loop about a quarter. Large errors are counted in full.

> Looping Lines must have a constant radius.
>
> [27.10.2](#rb-loops.radius)

> There are no standardized deductions for observed changes in the radius of Looping Lines. A judge must, therefore, develop a consistent and objective method for grading them.
>
> [27.10.4](#rb-loops.radius_deductions)

### Flat Spots in Loops {#radius_excitation}

`radius_excitation`

Checks that the loop has no straight sections. The share of the loop for which the flight path is effectively straight is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when the loop is high or wide in the box, when the direction towards the loop centre lies along the line of sight, and for part-loops that show less of the shape.

??? note "Details"

    Looping lines must have a constant radius, and where a roll is integrated into a loop any part of the roll flown on a straight line costs at least two points.

    FCScore watches the curvature of the flight path through the loop and counts the time during which it is effectively straight, or curving the wrong way. A local radius of about 1000 m or more counts as fully flat and about 500 m or less counts as curved, with values in between counting partly. The downgrade is based on the fraction of the loop's duration that is flat.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. These errors are easier to see when the direction from the aircraft towards the centre of the loop lies across the judge's line of sight, and harder when it lies along it. They are also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side, and the weighting is scaled by how much of a full loop is flown: a complete loop counts fully, a quarter loop about a quarter.

> Looping Lines must have a constant radius.
>
> [27.10.2](#rb-loops.radius)

> Rolls may appear on Looping Lines. The rolls must be centered symmetrically about the apex or nadir and be integrated into the radius. … If any part of the roll or roll combination is flown on a straight line, deduct at least two (2) points.
>
> [27.12.1-27.12.2](#rb-loops.integrated_rolls)

### Loop Rate of Turn {#curvature}

`curvature`

Checks that the loop keeps a steady rate of turn for its speed. The variation in the loop's curvature, compared with its average, is charged once for the loop. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when the loop is high or wide in the box, when the direction towards the loop centre lies along the line of sight, and for part-loops that show less of the shape.

??? note "Details"

    Looping lines must have a constant radius, which means the aircraft has to turn at a steady rate for its speed, neither tightening nor opening up as it goes round.

    FCScore measures the rate of turn divided by the speed of travel (the curvature, which is one over the radius) throughout the loop and calculates how much it varies as a fraction of its average. Because it is based on how quickly the aircraft is turning for its speed, it picks up a tightening or opening of the loop early. The more the curvature varies, the larger the downgrade.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. These errors are easier to see when the direction from the aircraft towards the centre of the loop lies across the judge's line of sight, and harder when it lies along it. They are also harder to judge high in the box or far to one side, and the weighting is scaled by how much of a full loop is flown: a complete loop counts fully, a quarter loop about a quarter.

> Looping Lines must have a constant radius.
>
> [27.10.2](#rb-loops.radius)

### Spin Rotation Axis {#spin_rotation_axis}

`spin_rotation_axis`

Checks that the spin is a true autorotation. Time spent rotating about an axis too close to the fuselage line, below 25°, is charged. Small errors are discounted only for aircraft that are high or wide in the box, where the angle is harder to judge.

??? note "Details"

    A spin is an autorotation after an aerodynamic stall, and if the aircraft does not stall or establish autorotation the figure is a hard zero. During autorotation pitch angle and rotation rate may vary without penalty, so only the type of rotation matters.

    FCScore measures the angle between the fuselage axis and the axis the aircraft is rotating about, from 15° after the break to 45° before the end of the rotation. Any period in which it is below 25° looks like a roll about the fuselage rather than an autorotation and is charged, according to how far below the limit it is and how large a share of the spin it covers. The 25° threshold is an FCScore way of detecting autorotation, not a number given in the rules.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. The visibility factors are the aircraft's position in the box (errors are harder to judge high in the box or far to one side) and a fixed balancing factor. Large errors are counted in full.

> A spin is an Autorotation performed on a steeply descending flight path following an aerodynamic stall. Spins only appear on vertical downlines.
>
> [28.24.1](#rb-spins.definition)

> At certain angles of attack, rudder input causes an aircraft to rotate about both the yaw and roll axes. The rotation continues if the rudder is continuously applied and the angle of attack is maintained, even if the ailerons are centered. This regime is called “autorotation”.
>
> [26.10.1](#rb-general.autorotation)

### Spin Nose Drop {#drop_pitch_rate}

`drop_pitch_rate`

Checks that the nose drops as the aircraft stalls into the spin. Time spent dropping slower than 6° per second in the first 15° of rotation is charged. Small shortfalls are discounted when hard to see: with the aircraft high or wide in the box, or directly above the judge.

??? note "Details"

    When the aircraft stalls it must move around all three axes at once: the nose pitches toward the ground, and the aircraft yaws and rolls. Failure to achieve simultaneous motion costs one point for every 5° of deviation.

    FCScore measures the nose-down pitch rate from the start of the spin until the first 15° of rotation is complete. Any period below 6° per second is charged, according to how far below it is and how large a share of that window it covers. The 6° per second figure is an FCScore threshold for a definite nose drop, not a number from the rules.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. The nose drop is harder to see when the aircraft is directly above the judge, and when it is high in the box or far to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales the error. Large errors are counted in full.

> When the aircraft stalls, the aircraft must simultaneously move around all three flight axes: a) the nose will pitch toward the ground; b) the aircraft will yaw; and c) the aircraft will roll. For failure to achieve simultaneous motion about all three axes, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of deviation.
>
> [28.24.2](#rb-spins.entry)

### Spin Rotation Hesitation {#spin_excitation}

`spin_excitation`

Checks that the spin keeps rotating. The share of the spin for which the rotation rate is very low is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see (aircraft viewed from above or below, or high or wide in the box) and short rotations count for less.

??? note "Details"

    Autorotation must continue throughout the spin. If it ceases before the end, one point is deducted for every 5° of rotation remaining, and the end of the rotation must not be completed with ailerons.

    FCScore counts the time in each spin during which the rotation rate in the correct direction is close to zero or reversed. A rate below about 9° per second counts as fully stopped, a rate above about 17° per second counts as rotating, and values in between count partly. The downgrade is based on the fraction of the spin's duration spent stopped.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. A stop in the rotation is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than from above or below, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. The weighting is also scaled by the amount of rotation flown, so a short rotation counts for less than a full one.

> Autorotation must continue throughout the spin. If the Autorotation ceases before the end of the spin, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of rotation remaining.
>
> [28.24.7](#rb-spins.continue)

### Spin Exit Pitch Attitude {#spin_exit_pitch}

`spin_exit_pitch`

Checks that the aircraft ends the spin pointing vertically down in pitch. The full pitch angle error of the fuselage at the end of the spin is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    A vertical downline must be established at the same time as, or shortly after, the autorotation stops, and the aircraft must stop rotating precisely on the axis. Alignment errors cost one point for every 5°.

    FCScore takes the last point of the spin and charges the whole angle between the fuselage and the template downline in the pitch direction. It is an absolute measure at that point. This is based on the direction the nose points (the attitude). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> A vertical downline must be established at the same time as, or shortly after, the cessation of autorotation.
>
> [28.24.8](#rb-spins.downline)

> After completion of the prescribed number of turns, the aircraft must stop rotating precisely on either the X or Y axis and in the direction of flight appropriate to the sequence being flown. If the aircraft does not end up with the correct alignment, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of error.
>
> [28.24.6](#rb-spins.stop)

### Spin Exit Sideways Lean {#spin_exit_yaw}

`spin_exit_yaw`

Checks that the aircraft ends the spin pointing vertically down, not leaning to the side. The full sideways angle error of the fuselage at the end of the spin is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    After the prescribed turns the aircraft must stop rotating precisely on the X or Y axis, with a vertical downline established. Alignment errors cost one point for every 5°.

    FCScore takes the last point of the spin and charges the whole sideways angle between the fuselage and the template downline. It is an absolute measure at that point. This is based on the direction the nose points (the attitude). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> After completion of the prescribed number of turns, the aircraft must stop rotating precisely on either the X or Y axis and in the direction of flight appropriate to the sequence being flown. If the aircraft does not end up with the correct alignment, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of error.
>
> [28.24.6](#rb-spins.stop)

> A vertical downline must be established at the same time as, or shortly after, the cessation of autorotation.
>
> [28.24.8](#rb-spins.downline)

### Snap Rotation Axis {#snap_rotation_axis}

`snap_rotation_axis`

Checks that the snap is a true autorotation rather than an axial roll. Time spent rotating about an axis too close to the fuselage line, below 10°, is charged. Small errors are discounted only for aircraft that are high or wide in the box, where the angle is harder to judge.

??? note "Details"

    A snap roll is an autorotation at a high angle of attack, with pitch and yaw as well as roll visible, so the rotation should not be a simple roll about the fuselage line.

    FCScore measures the angle between the fuselage axis and the axis the aircraft is rotating about, from 15° after the start of the rotation to 90° before its end. Any period in which it is below 10° looks like an aileron roll and is charged, according to how far below the limit it is and how large a share of the snap it covers. The threshold is an FCScore way of detecting autorotation, not a number given in the rules.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. The visibility factors are the aircraft's position in the box (errors are harder to judge high in the box or far to one side) and a fixed balancing factor. Large errors are counted in full.

> A snap roll is an Autorotation at a high angle of attack.
>
> [28.22.1](#rb-snap_rolls.definition)

> At certain angles of attack, rudder input causes an aircraft to rotate about both the yaw and roll axes. The rotation continues if the rudder is continuously applied and the angle of attack is maintained, even if the ailerons are centered. This regime is called “autorotation”.
>
> [26.10.1](#rb-general.autorotation)

### Snap Rotation Hesitation {#snap_excitation}

`snap_excitation`

Checks that the snap keeps rotating. The share of the snap for which the rotation rate is low is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see (aircraft viewed from above or below, or high or wide in the box) and short rotations count for less.

??? note "Details"

    Autorotation must continue throughout the snap. If it ceases before the end of the roll, one point is deducted for every 5° of rotation remaining.

    FCScore counts the time in each snap during which the rotation rate in the correct direction is low. A rate below about 30° per second counts as fully stopped, a rate above about 57° per second counts as rotating, and values in between count partly. The downgrade is based on the fraction of the snap's duration spent stopped.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. A stop in the rotation is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than from above or below, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. The weighting is also scaled by the amount of rotation flown, so a short rotation counts for less than a full one.

> Throughout the snap, the Autorotation must continue. If the Autorotation ceases before the end of the roll, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of rotation remaining.
>
> [28.22.7](#rb-snap_rolls.autorotation)

### Positive Snap Pitch Break {#pos_break_pr}

`pos_break_pr`

Checks that a positive snap starts with a clear pitch break. If the peak pitch rate in the first 15° of rotation never reaches 30° per second, the shortfall is charged. Small shortfalls are discounted when hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, or when it is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    To show a positive snap has been correctly initiated the judge must see a rapid and clearly visible pitch rotation in the nose up / tail down sense, followed by visible yaw and autorotation.

    FCScore looks at the pitch rate over the first 15° of the rotation and takes its largest absolute value. If that peak never reaches 30° per second the shortfall is charged. The 30° per second figure is an FCScore threshold for a clear break, not a number from the rules, and only the peak counts.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Pitch rate is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than when you are looking at its top or underside, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales the error.

> The judge must see two things to determine that a positive snap roll has been correctly initiated: a) a rapid and clearly visible pitch rotation in the nose up / tail down sense. b) visible yaw rotation followed by Autorotation.
>
> [28.22.2](#rb-snap_rolls.break)

### Negative Snap Pitch Break {#neg_break_pr}

`neg_break_pr`

Checks that a negative snap starts with a clear pitch break. The peak pitch rate in the first 15° of rotation is compared with a 30° per second threshold and any shortfall is charged. Small shortfalls are discounted when hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, or when it is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    A negative snap roll uses the same criteria as a positive one except that the nose and tail must initially move in the nose down / tail up sense, with a rapid and clearly visible pitch rotation.

    FCScore looks at the pitch rate over the first 15° of the rotation and compares its absolute value with a 30° per second threshold, charging any shortfall. The threshold is an FCScore value for a clear break, not a number from the rules.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Pitch rate is easier to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on than when you are looking at its top or underside, and easier in front of the judge than high in the box or far to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales the error.

> For negative snap rolls, all criteria stated for positive snap rolls apply except in a negative snap roll the nose and tail of the aircraft must initially move in the nose down / tail up sense.
>
> [28.23.1](#rb-snap_rolls.negative)

> The judge must see two things to determine that a positive snap roll has been correctly initiated: a) a rapid and clearly visible pitch rotation in the nose up / tail down sense. b) visible yaw rotation followed by Autorotation.
>
> [28.22.2](#rb-snap_rolls.break)

### Snap Exit Pitch Attitude {#snap_exit_pitch}

`snap_exit_pitch`

Checks that the aircraft returns to the correct pitch attitude after a snap on a vertical or 45° line. Only growth in the pitch error between the start and end of the snap is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    At the end of a snap the aircraft must immediately adopt the attitude that fits the underlying figure, and failing to re-establish it costs one point for every 5°. A lateral or vertical displacement of the path caused by the snap is not charged provided the path stays parallel.

    FCScore compares the fuselage pitch relative to the template at the first and last points of the snap and charges any increase in the absolute error between them. A snap that leaves the attitude closer to the template than it started is free, and an error present before the snap is not charged again. It applies to snaps that do not finish on a horizontal line. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> At the conclusion of the snap the aircraft must immediately adopt the attitude or flight path that conforms to the requirements of the underlying figure. If the original attitude or flight path angle is not reestablished, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees.
>
> [28.22.8](#rb-snap_rolls.exit)

### Snap Exit Yaw Attitude {#snap_exit_yaw}

`snap_exit_yaw`

Checks that the aircraft returns to the correct heading after a snap on a vertical or 45° line. Only growth in the yaw error between the start and end of the snap is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    At the end of a snap the aircraft must immediately adopt the attitude that fits the underlying figure, and failing to re-establish it costs one point for every 5°. A lateral or vertical displacement of the path caused by the snap is not charged provided the path stays parallel.

    FCScore compares the fuselage yaw relative to the template at the first and last points of the snap and charges any increase in the absolute error between them. A snap that leaves the attitude closer to the template than it started is free, and an error present before the snap is not charged again. It applies to snaps that do not finish on a horizontal line. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> At the conclusion of the snap the aircraft must immediately adopt the attitude or flight path that conforms to the requirements of the underlying figure. If the original attitude or flight path angle is not reestablished, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees.
>
> [28.22.8](#rb-snap_rolls.exit)

### Snap Exit Climb Angle {#snap_exit_climb}

`snap_exit_climb`

Checks that the flight path returns to level after a snap that finishes on a horizontal line. Only growth in the climb or descent angle between the start and end of the snap is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    At the end of a snap the aircraft must immediately adopt the flight path that fits the underlying figure, and horizontal lines are judged on flight path. Failing to re-establish it costs one point for every 5°.

    FCScore compares the flight path angle to the horizontal at the first and last points of the snap and charges any increase in the absolute error between them. A snap that leaves the path closer to the template than it started is free, and an error present before the snap is not charged again. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> At the conclusion of the snap the aircraft must immediately adopt the attitude or flight path that conforms to the requirements of the underlying figure. If the original attitude or flight path angle is not reestablished, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees.

### Snap Exit Heading {#snap_exit_heading}

`snap_exit_heading`

Checks that the heading returns to the box axis after a snap that finishes on a horizontal line. Only growth in the heading error between the start and end of the snap is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    At the end of a snap the aircraft must immediately adopt the attitude that fits the underlying figure, and on a horizontal line the heading must remain parallel to the box axis. Failing to re-establish it costs one point for every 5°.

    FCScore compares the fuselage heading relative to the template at the first and last points of the snap and charges any increase in the absolute error between them. A snap that leaves the heading closer to the template than it started is free, and an error present before the snap is not charged again. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> At the conclusion of the snap the aircraft must immediately adopt the attitude or flight path that conforms to the requirements of the underlying figure. If the original attitude or flight path angle is not reestablished, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees.
>
> [28.22.8](#rb-snap_rolls.exit)

> The aircraft’s heading must remain parallel to the X or Y axis.
>
> [27.5.2](#rb-lines.heading)

### Stall Turn Pivot Width {#width}

`width`

Checks that the aircraft pivots near its centre of gravity at the top of a stall turn. The sideways travel in the direction of the turn beyond an allowance is charged, ignoring downwind drift. Small errors are discounted when hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or when the aircraft is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    During the pivot the aircraft's centre of gravity may move up to half a wingspan without penalty, and each additional half wingspan of displacement costs one point. Lateral movement caused by wind drift is not charged.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft's centre of gravity moves sideways in the direction of the turn from the start of the stall turn, with movement from drifting downwind removed but upwind drift left in. The largest width beyond a fixed allowance is charged once. FCScore uses a fixed distance rather than your wingspan, so it approximates the wingspan-based rule, and it charges smoothly rather than in half-wingspan steps.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight than across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. Large errors are counted in full.

> The pivot begins when the aircraft starts to yaw or when it starts to backslide prior to yaw. The pivot ends when the aircraft is established on the downline. During the pivot, the aircraft's CG may displace by up to one-half wingspan without penalty. The penalty for any additional displacement, either laterally or vertically, is one point per half wingspan.
>
> [28.8.3](#rb-stall_turns.pivot)

> During the pivot, there is no deduction for any CG lateral motion caused by wind drift.
>
> [28.8.5](#rb-stall_turns.wind_drift)

### Stall Turn Height Loss {#height}

`height`

Checks that the aircraft does not lose height through the pivot of a stall turn. How far below its highest point the aircraft is at the start and end of the stall turn, beyond an allowance, is charged. Small errors are discounted when hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or when the aircraft is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    During the pivot the aircraft's centre of gravity may move up to half a wingspan without penalty, and each additional half wingspan of displacement, laterally or vertically, costs one point.

    FCScore measures how far below the highest point of the stall turn the aircraft is at the first and last points of the stall turn element, and charges any height lost beyond a fixed allowance. FCScore uses a fixed distance rather than your wingspan, so it approximates the wingspan-based rule, and it charges smoothly rather than in half-wingspan steps.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight than across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. Large errors are counted in full.

> The pivot begins when the aircraft starts to yaw or when it starts to backslide prior to yaw. The pivot ends when the aircraft is established on the downline. During the pivot, the aircraft's CG may displace by up to one-half wingspan without penalty. The penalty for any additional displacement, either laterally or vertically, is one point per half wingspan.
>
> [28.8.3](#rb-stall_turns.pivot)

### Stall Turn Downline Yaw {#stallturn_exit_yaw}

`stallturn_exit_yaw`

Checks that the downline after a stall turn is not leaning sideways. The full sideways attitude error at the end of the line is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    After the pivot the aircraft must be established on a vertical downline, which like all vertical lines is judged on attitude, at one point per 5° of error.

    FCScore takes the last point of the line that follows the stall turn and charges the whole sideways angle between the fuselage and the template. It is an absolute measure at the end of the line. This is based on the direction the nose points (the attitude). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Vertical lines are judged on the attitude of the aircraft, according to its zero-lift axis, and not the flight path.
>
> [27.3.1](#rb-lines.vertical)

> The pivot begins when the aircraft starts to yaw or when it starts to backslide prior to yaw. The pivot ends when the aircraft is established on the downline. The penalty for any additional displacement, either laterally or vertically, is one point per half wingspan.

### Tailslide Sideways Lean {#tailslide_yaw}

`tailslide_yaw`

Checks that the aircraft does not lean sideways during a tailslide. Only growth in the sideways lean of the fuselage is charged. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    A tailslide climbs vertically, stops and slides backwards vertically. Pilots commonly lean into the slide to control the pivot direction, but the standard deduction of one point for every 5° of deviation still applies.

    FCScore measures the lean of the fuselage sideways relative to the template throughout the tailslide and charges each increase in the absolute angle; a decrease is free. This is based on the direction the nose points (the attitude). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Leaning into the slide to better control the pivot direction is common practice. Regardless, the standard deduction of one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of deviation applies.
>
> [28.9.1](#rb-tailslides.lean)

### Tailslide Exit Pitch {#tailslide_exit_pitch}

`tailslide_exit_pitch`

Checks that the aircraft finishes the tailslide pointing vertically down in pitch. The full pitch attitude error at the end of the tailslide is charged once. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    After the backwards slide the aircraft must pivot in the correct direction to a vertical down position, and may swing past the vertical before establishing the downline.

    FCScore takes the last point of the tailslide and charges the whole pitch angle between the fuselage and the template. It is an absolute measure at that point, so a swing past the vertical that has settled by then is not charged. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Following the backwards slide, the aircraft must then pivot in the correct direction to a vertical down position.
>
> [28.9.4](#rb-tailslides.recovery)

### Tailslide Stop {#tailslide_stop}

`tailslide_stop`

Checks that the aircraft comes to a stop at the top of the vertical line before it slides back. The vertical speed left at the end of the upline is charged once. Small errors are discounted when hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or when the aircraft is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    In a tailslide the aircraft climbs vertically and stops before sliding backwards, with the backwards slide beginning when upward motion ceases.

    FCScore takes the last point of the line before the tailslide and charges the absolute vertical speed there. A larger speed means the aircraft was still climbing, or already falling, instead of being stopped. The downgrade scale is an FCScore value; the rules do not set a speed limit.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight than across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. Large errors are counted in full.

> In a tailslide, the aircraft climbs vertically, stops, and slides backwards vertically before pivoting on the pitch axis to recover in a vertical down line.
>
> [28.9.1](#rb-tailslides.definition)

### Tailslide Slide Distance {#tailslide_drop}

`tailslide_drop`

Checks that the aircraft slides backwards a visible distance. A slide shorter than 1 m is charged. Small errors are discounted when hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or when the aircraft is high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    The aircraft must slide backwards at least half a fuselage length; if it does not the figure is a hard zero.

    FCScore adds up the distance travelled backwards through the tailslide and charges any shortfall below 1 m. FCScore uses a fixed distance rather than your fuselage length, and charges a graded downgrade rather than the hard zero given in the rules.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight than across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. Large errors are counted in full.

> The backwards slide begins when the aircraft ceases upward motion. The aircraft must slide backwards at least one-half of the fuselage length. If it fails to do so, mark the figure HZ.
>
> [28.9.3](#rb-tailslides.slide)

### Sequence Entry Climb {#seqstart_entry_climb}

`seqstart_entry_climb`

Checks the climb angle before the first figure. The error at the start of the window, just before the figure, is charged in full. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, or high or wide in the box.

??? note "Details"

    Figures begin in wings-level, horizontal flight aligned with a box axis. Nothing is judged before the first figure of a sequence, so FCScore looks at the last second of the line before it, to make sure the aircraft enters the figure level and aligned and does not dive, climb or bank into it.

    FCScore takes the sample one second before the start of the first element of the figure and charges the whole angle between the flight path and the horizontal. It is an absolute measure because nothing earlier has been charged. The window length is a tuning setting (one second by default). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Figures begin and end in wings-level, horizontal flight, aligned with a box axis.
>
> [26.1.8](#rb-general.figure_start)

> Horizontal lines are to be flown at a constant altitude and judged on flight path, not attitude.
>
> [27.5.1](#rb-lines.horizontal)

### Sequence Entry Climb Drift {#seqstart_climb}

`seqstart_climb`

Checks the climb angle stays correct before the first figure. Only growth in the error over the window next to the figure is charged, so a correction back towards the template is free.     Figures begin in wings-level, horizontal flight aligned with a box axis. Nothing is judged before the first figure of a sequence, so FCScore looks at the last second of the line before it, to make sure the aircraft enters the figure level and aligned and does not dive, climb or bank into it.

    FCScore measures the angle between the flight path and the horizontal over the last second of the line before the figure and charges each increase in the absolute error; a decrease is free. An error already present at the start of the window is charged by the matching check at that point, not again here. The window ends where the figure starts and moves with it, so the error cannot be moved out of the score by placing the start of the figure later. The window length is a tuning setting (one second by default). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, and when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Figures begin and end in wings-level, horizontal flight, aligned with a box axis.
