`seqend_heading`

Checks the heading stays correct after the last figure. Only growth in the error over the window next to the figure is charged, so a correction back towards the template is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: along the judge's line of sight, high or wide in the box, or on awkward line angles.

??? note "Details"

    Figures end in wings-level, horizontal flight aligned with a box axis. Nothing is judged after the last figure of a sequence, so FCScore looks at the first second of the line after it, to make sure the aircraft leaves the figure level and aligned and does not overshoot, dive, climb or bank away from it.

    FCScore measures the angle between the fuselage and the template heading in the horizontal plane, which measures the nose rather than the flight path over the first second of the line after the figure and charges each increase in the absolute error; a decrease is free. An error already present at the start of the window is charged by the matching check at the end of the figure, not again here. The window starts where the figure ends and moves with it, so an overshoot cannot be moved out of the score by ending the figure earlier. The window length is a tuning setting (one second by default). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. An error is harder to see when it lies along the judge's line of sight (the aircraft moving or pointing towards or away from the judge) than when it lies across it, when the aircraft is high in the box or far off to one side, and when the correct line is at an angle that is hard to picture: horizontal and vertical lines are the easiest to judge, 45° lines are harder and the angles in between are hardest. A fixed balancing factor also scales these errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Figures begin and end in wings-level, horizontal flight, aligned with a box axis.
>
> [26.1.8](#rb-general.figure_start)

> The aircraft’s heading must remain parallel to the X or Y axis.
>
> [27.5.2](#rb-lines.heading)

### Sequence Exit Wings Level {#seqend_exit_roll}

`seqend_exit_roll`

Checks the roll angle after the last figure. The error at the end of the figure is charged in full. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    Figures end in wings-level, horizontal flight aligned with a box axis. Nothing is judged after the last figure of a sequence, so FCScore looks at the first second of the line after it, to make sure the aircraft leaves the figure level and aligned and does not overshoot, dive, climb or bank away from it.

    FCScore takes the last point of the figure, the start of the exit line, and charges the whole difference between the aircraft's roll angle and the template attitude. It is an absolute measure because nothing earlier has been charged. FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Figures begin and end in wings-level, horizontal flight, aligned with a box axis.
>
> [26.1.8](#rb-general.figure_start)

> Deduct 0.5 points for every 2.5 degrees of angular error or fraction thereof.
>
> [27.6.1](#rb-general.angle_rule)

### Sequence Exit Roll Angle {#seqend_roll}

`seqend_roll`

Checks the roll angle stays correct after the last figure. Only growth in the error over the window next to the figure is charged, so a correction back towards the template is free. Small errors are discounted when they are hard to see: when you are looking at the top or underside of the aircraft, when it is high or wide in the box, or at awkward bank angles.

??? note "Details"

    Figures end in wings-level, horizontal flight aligned with a box axis. Nothing is judged after the last figure of a sequence, so FCScore looks at the first second of the line after it, to make sure the aircraft leaves the figure level and aligned and does not overshoot, dive, climb or bank away from it.

    FCScore measures the difference between the aircraft's roll angle and the template attitude over the first second of the line after the figure and charges each increase in the absolute error; a decrease is free. An error already present at the start of the window is charged by the matching check at the end of the figure, not again here. The window starts where the figure ends and moves with it, so an overshoot cannot be moved out of the score by ending the figure earlier. The window length is a tuning setting (one second by default). FCScore's scale is calibrated to roughly one point per 5° of error, in line with the IAC rule.

    Visibility only ever reduces how much of a small error is charged. Roll errors are easiest to see when the aircraft is viewed side-on and hardest when you are looking at its top or underside. They are also harder to judge when the aircraft is high in the box or far to one side, and when the bank angle or the line is awkward to picture: wings level, knife-edge and inverted are the easiest references, with the angles in between the hardest. A fixed balancing factor, smaller than for flight path errors, further reduces small roll errors. Large errors are counted in full.

> Figures begin and end in wings-level, horizontal flight, aligned with a box axis.
>
> [26.1.8](#rb-general.figure_start)

> Deduct 0.5 points for every 2.5 degrees of angular error or fraction thereof.
>
> [27.6.1](#rb-general.angle_rule)

## Positioning (box) downgrades

### Box Ceiling {#top}

`top`

Checks that the figure stays below the top of the aerobatic box. The distance above the ceiling, averaged over the duration of the figure, is charged, so a small or brief excursion costs little. Small excursions that are hard to see are discounted.

??? note "Details"

    Competitors must obey the altitude limits for their category, and a figure with any portion above the ceiling of the aerobatic box receives a HIGH infringement penalty. The ceiling depends on the category flown.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft is above the ceiling of the box over the whole figure. Each stretch above is charged in proportion to how far above it is and for how much of the figure's duration. The rules apply a fixed contest penalty per figure rather than a graded deduction, so this is an FCScore estimate of the severity of the infringement.

    Visibility is based on the direction of the error compared with the direction of view: an error that lies along the line of sight is hard to see, one across it is easier, so small excursions are discounted when they are hard to see. Large excursions are counted in full.

> HIGH: Assessed if any portion of the figure is above the ceiling of the aerobatic box.
>
> [13.5.1](#rb-box.ceiling)

### Right Box Boundary {#right}

`right`

Checks that the figure stays inside the the right boundary of the aerobatic box. The distance outside the boundary, averaged over the duration of the figure, is charged, so a small or brief excursion costs little. Small excursions that are hard to see are discounted.

??? note "Details"

    The aerobatic box is a clearly marked area 1,000 m square, and flying any part of a figure outside the lateral boundaries carries a boundary infringement penalty, with only one such penalty per figure.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft is outside the right boundary of the box over the whole figure. Each stretch outside is charged in proportion to how far out it is and for how much of the figure's duration. The rules apply a fixed contest penalty per figure rather than a graded deduction, so this is an FCScore estimate of the severity of the infringement.

    Visibility is based on the direction of the error compared with the direction of view: an error that lies along the line of sight is hard to see, one across it is easier, so small excursions are discounted when they are hard to see. Large excursions are counted in full.

> Performances occur above a clearly marked area of 1,000 meters (approximately 3,280 feet) square whose central point is the intersection of the X and Y axes.
>
> [7.1.1](#rb-box.limits)

> The penalties for flying any part of a figure outside the lateral boundaries of the Aerobatic Box are:
>
> [13.2.1](#rb-box.boundary_penalty)

### Left Box Boundary {#left}

`left`

Checks that the figure stays inside the the left boundary of the aerobatic box. The distance outside the boundary, averaged over the duration of the figure, is charged, so a small or brief excursion costs little. Small excursions that are hard to see are discounted.

??? note "Details"

    The aerobatic box is a clearly marked area 1,000 m square, and flying any part of a figure outside the lateral boundaries carries a boundary infringement penalty, with only one such penalty per figure.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft is outside the left boundary of the box over the whole figure. Each stretch outside is charged in proportion to how far out it is and for how much of the figure's duration. The rules apply a fixed contest penalty per figure rather than a graded deduction, so this is an FCScore estimate of the severity of the infringement.

    Visibility is based on the direction of the error compared with the direction of view: an error that lies along the line of sight is hard to see, one across it is easier, so small excursions are discounted when they are hard to see. Large excursions are counted in full.

> Performances occur above a clearly marked area of 1,000 meters (approximately 3,280 feet) square whose central point is the intersection of the X and Y axes.
>
> [7.1.1](#rb-box.limits)

> The penalties for flying any part of a figure outside the lateral boundaries of the Aerobatic Box are:
>
> [13.2.1](#rb-box.boundary_penalty)

### Back Box Boundary {#back}

`back`

Checks that the figure stays inside the back boundary of the aerobatic box. The distance beyond the boundary, averaged over the duration of the figure, is charged, so a small or brief excursion costs little. Small excursions that are hard to see are discounted.

??? note "Details"

    The aerobatic box is a clearly marked area 1,000 m square, and flying any part of a figure outside its boundaries carries a boundary infringement penalty, with only one such penalty per figure. A figure that cannot be properly graded because of viewing distance also loses 2 points.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft is beyond the back boundary of the box over the whole figure. Each stretch outside is charged in proportion to how far out it is and for how much of the figure's duration. The rules apply a fixed contest penalty per figure rather than a graded deduction, so this is an FCScore estimate of the severity of the infringement.

    Visibility is based on the direction of the error compared with the direction of view: an error that lies along the line of sight is hard to see, one across it is easier, so small excursions are discounted when they are hard to see. Large excursions are counted in full.

> Performances occur above a clearly marked area of 1,000 meters (approximately 3,280 feet) square whose central point is the intersection of the X and Y axes.
>
> [7.1.1](#rb-box.limits)

> For each figure that cannot be properly graded because of viewing angle or distance, deduct 2 points.
>
> [27.15.1](#rb-box.scorability)

### Front Box Boundary {#front}

`front`

Checks that the figure stays behind the front boundary of the aerobatic box. The distance in front of the boundary, averaged over the duration of the figure, is charged, so a small or brief excursion costs little. Small excursions that are hard to see are discounted.

??? note "Details"

    The aerobatic box is a clearly marked area 1,000 m square, and flying any part of a figure outside its boundaries carries a boundary infringement penalty, with only one such penalty per figure.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft is in front of the front boundary of the box over the whole figure. Each stretch outside is charged in proportion to how far out it is and for how much of the figure's duration. The rules apply a fixed contest penalty per figure rather than a graded deduction, so this is an FCScore estimate of the severity of the infringement.

    Visibility is based on the direction of the error compared with the direction of view: an error that lies along the line of sight is hard to see, one across it is easier, so small excursions are discounted when they are hard to see. Large excursions are counted in full.

> Performances occur above a clearly marked area of 1,000 meters (approximately 3,280 feet) square whose central point is the intersection of the X and Y axes.
>
> [7.1.1](#rb-box.limits)

> The penalties for flying any part of a figure outside the lateral boundaries of the Aerobatic Box are:
>
> [13.2.1](#rb-box.boundary_penalty)

### Box Floor {#btm}

`btm`

Checks that the figure stays above the floor of the aerobatic box. The distance below the floor, averaged over the duration of the figure, is charged heavily. Small excursions that are hard to see are discounted.

??? note "Details"

    Competitors must obey the altitude limits for their category, and a figure with any portion below the floor of the aerobatic box receives a LOW infringement penalty; an unsafe altitude far below the floor zeroes the performance. The floor depends on the category flown.

    FCScore measures how far the aircraft is below the floor of the box over the whole figure. Each stretch below is charged in proportion to how far below it is and for how much of the figure's duration, on a steeper scale than the other box limits. The rules apply fixed contest penalties rather than a graded deduction, so this is an FCScore estimate of the severity of the infringement.

    Visibility is based on the direction of the error compared with the direction of view: an error that lies along the line of sight is hard to see, one across it is easier, so small excursions are discounted when they are hard to see. Large excursions are counted in full.

> LOW: Assessed if any portion of the figure is below the floor of the aerobatic box.
>
> [13.5.1](#rb-box.floor)

## Inter-element downgrades

### Loop Radius Matching {#inter.loop_radius}

`inter.loop_radius`

Checks that the looping lines in a figure that must have matching radii do match. Each radius is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    Only certain figures require matching radii, such as the combinations of lines in Family 3, segmented loops, reversing loops, S's and eights; where the rule applies all matching radii must be the same size as the first. IAC has no standardized downgrade for a mismatch.

    FCScore takes the radius of each looping line the figure requires to match and compares each with the previous one, rather than with the first, charging in proportion to how many times larger one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the size. Whether each loop is round is judged by Loop Roundness.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> For figures containing more than one Looping Line, there may be an additional requirement for two or more of them to have matching radii.
>
> [27.13.1](#rb-loops.matching_radii)

> All matching radii must be the same size as the first radius.
>
> [27.13.5](#rb-loops.radius_basis)

### Line Length Matching {#inter.line_length}

`inter.line_length`

Checks that lines that must be of equal length in a figure are. Each length is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    Interior lines do not have to be equal unless the figure says so, as in Family 3 and the square and octagon loops. Where equal lengths are required, a visible variation of less than 2:1 costs one point, 2:1 to 3:1 two points, and 3:1 or more three points, with the first line flown as the basis.

    FCScore takes the length of each line the figure requires to match and compares each with the previous one, charging in proportion to how many times longer one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the length. FCScore's scale is smooth rather than in the rulebook's steps.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> If within a figure, two or more Interior Lines, or Line Segments, must be of the same length, an observed variation is penalized by reducing the grade in the following manner: … a visible variation less than 2:1 - 1 point deduction; … variation from 2:1 but less than 3:1 - 2 point deduction; … variation of 3:1 or more - 3 point deduction;
>
> [27.9.4](#rb-lines.length_penalty)

> The basis for judging line length is the first Interior Line or Line Segment flown.
>
> [27.9.5](#rb-lines.length_basis)

### Roll Rate Matching {#inter.roll_rate}

`inter.roll_rate`

Checks that the rolls within one roll combination are flown at the same roll rate. Each rate is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    IAC requires the rates between the points of a hesitation roll to match, and each rate that differs from the first costs one point. It does not require the rotation rates of unlinked rolls to match each other, so this is the rule it follows most closely for hesitation rolls.

    FCScore takes the roll rate of each roll within a roll combination on the same line and compares each with the previous one, charging in proportion to how many times faster one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the rate. FCScore groups rolls by the figure definition rather than by the rule, so check the rulebook for your figure. Whether the rate is steady within one roll is judged by Roll Rate Consistency.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> The rates of roll between each point must match. For each roll rate observed to be different from the first, deduct one (1) point.
>
> [28.21.3](#rb-rolls.hesitation_rate)

### Pause Duration Matching {#inter.point_duration}

`inter.point_duration`

Checks that the pauses between the rolls or points of a roll combination last the same time. Each duration is compared with the one before it and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    In a hesitation roll the duration of the pause at each point must match, and each pause that differs from the first costs one point. Unlinked rolls must also show a brief pause between them.

    FCScore takes the duration of each pause in a roll combination on the same line and compares each with the previous one, charging in proportion to how many times longer one is than the other. A pair that matches scores zero, whatever the duration.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> The duration of the pauses at each point must match. For each pause duration observed to be different from the first, deduct one (1) point.
>
> [28.21.4](#rb-rolls.hesitation_pause)

> The rolls must have a brief pause between them.
>
> [27.8.2](#rb-rolls.unlinked_pause)

### Roll Position On Line {#inter.pad_length}

`inter.pad_length`

Checks that a roll is centred on its line, with equal lengths of line before and after it. The two lengths are compared and the percentage difference is charged. Differences are discounted for small elements, which are harder to compare: visibility rises with the distance flown relative to the height of the box.

??? note "Details"

    If any kind of roll is placed on an interior line, the lengths of the two parts of the line before and after the roll must be equal, with the same penalties as other equal-length lines.

    FCScore compares the length of line before the roll with the length after, charging in proportion to how many times longer one is than the other. A roll that is perfectly centred scores zero, whatever the length of the line.

    Visibility scales the whole downgrade, not only small differences. Each comparison is weighted by how large the elements are compared with the height of the aerobatic box, taking the more visible of the two elements being compared: an element that fills the box is fully visible, while a small one is proportionally harder to judge against its neighbour.

> If any kind of roll is placed on an Interior Line, the lengths of the two parts of the line (Line Segments) before and after the roll must be equal.
>
> [27.9.3](#rb-lines.length_equal)

> If within a figure, two or more Interior Lines, or Line Segments, must be of the same length, an observed variation is penalized by reducing the grade in the following manner: … a visible variation less than 2:1 - 1 point deduction; … variation from 2:1 but less than 3:1 - 2 point deduction; … variation of 3:1 or more - 3 point deduction;
>
> [27.9.4](#rb-lines.length_penalty)

## Rulebook references

### 13.2.1 {#rb-box.boundary_penalty}

`box.boundary_penalty`

> The penalties for flying any part of a figure outside the lateral boundaries of the Aerobatic Box are:

### 13.2.2 {#rb-box.one_penalty}

`box.one_penalty`

> Only one Boundary Infringement Penalty may be assessed per figure.

### 13.5.1 {#rb-box.ceiling}

`box.ceiling`

> HIGH: Assessed if any portion of the figure is above the ceiling of the aerobatic box.

### 13.5.1 {#rb-box.floor}

`box.floor`

> LOW: Assessed if any portion of the figure is below the floor of the aerobatic box.

### 26.1.3 {#rb-general.grading}

`general.grading`

> A grade of ten (10.0) represents a perfect figure in which the judge saw no deviations from the prescribed criteria.

### 26.1.8 {#rb-general.figure_start}

`general.figure_start`

> Figures begin and end in wings-level, horizontal flight, aligned with a box axis.

### 26.1.9 {#rb-general.grading_window}

`general.grading_window`

> The grading of each figure begins upon departure from horizontal flight and ends upon resumption of horizontal flight.

### 26.10.1 {#rb-general.autorotation}

`general.autorotation`

> At certain angles of attack, rudder input causes an aircraft to rotate about both the yaw and roll axes. The rotation continues if the rudder is continuously applied and the angle of attack is maintained, even if the ailerons are centered. This regime is called “autorotation”.

### 26.6.2 {#rb-general.corrections}

`general.corrections`

> Downgrades are always made for the original error but not for any corrections which immediately follow.

### 26.6.3 {#rb-general.entry_geometry}

`general.entry_geometry`

> When a downgrade in geometry (pitch, roll, yaw) is observed for one element within a figure, any immediately following element within the same figure is not downgraded a second time for any misaligned entry geometry.

### 26.8.1 {#rb-general.no_line_between}

`general.no_line_between`

> If there is no discernible horizontal line between figures, deduct one (1) point from each figure.

### 27.1.1 {#rb-general.flight_path}

`general.flight_path`

> The Flight Path is the movement of the aircraft’s center of gravity through the sky. Judging the flight path consists of comparing the observed path with fixed references such as the horizon or the X and Y axes of the Aerobatic Box.

### 27.10.2 {#rb-loops.radius}

`loops.radius`

> Looping Lines must have a constant radius.

### 27.10.3 {#rb-loops.crosswind}

`loops.crosswind`

> The wind correction requirement is only regarding the roundness of the Looping Line and not for the effect of crosswind. Therefore, no deduction is given if the finish point is displaced relative to the start point in a direction perpendicular to the plane of the loop.

### 27.10.4 {#rb-loops.radius_deductions}

`loops.radius_deductions`

> There are no standardized deductions for observed changes in the radius of Looping Lines. A judge must, therefore, develop a consistent and objective method for grading them.

### 27.12.1-27.12.2 {#rb-loops.integrated_rolls}

`loops.integrated_rolls`

> Rolls may appear on Looping Lines. The rolls must be centered symmetrically about the apex or nadir and be integrated into the radius. … If any part of the roll or roll combination is flown on a straight line, deduct at least two (2) points.

### 27.13.1 {#rb-loops.matching_radii}

`loops.matching_radii`

> For figures containing more than one Looping Line, there may be an additional requirement for two or more of them to have matching radii.

### 27.13.5 {#rb-loops.radius_basis}

`loops.radius_basis`

> All matching radii must be the same size as the first radius.

### 27.14.1 {#rb-general.wind_correction}

`general.wind_correction`

> Competitors may attempt to correct for wind drift but if these corrections are visible to the judge the standard deduction of one (1) point per five (5) degrees of heading deviation must be given.

### 27.15.1 {#rb-box.scorability}

`box.scorability`

> For each figure that cannot be properly graded because of viewing angle or distance, deduct 2 points.

### 27.3.1 {#rb-lines.vertical}

`lines.vertical`

> Vertical lines are judged on the attitude of the aircraft, according to its zero-lift axis, and not the flight path.

### 27.3.2 {#rb-lines.vertical_wings}

`lines.vertical_wings`

> The wings must be aligned with a box axis and the horizon.

### 27.4.1 {#rb-lines.diagonal}

`lines.diagonal`

> 45 Degree lines are judged according to the perfect vertical attitude plus or minus 45 degrees.

### 27.5.1 {#rb-lines.horizontal}

`lines.horizontal`

> Horizontal lines are to be flown at a constant altitude and judged on flight path, not attitude.

### 27.5.2 {#rb-lines.heading}

`lines.heading`

> The aircraft’s heading must remain parallel to the X or Y axis.

### 27.6.1 {#rb-general.angle_rule}

`general.angle_rule`

> Deduct 0.5 points for every 2.5 degrees of angular error or fraction thereof.

### 27.7.1 {#rb-general.proportional}

`general.proportional`

> In cases where a specific deduction value is not specified, the judge shall apply a deduction proportional to the error.

### 27.8.2 {#rb-rolls.unlinked_pause}

`rolls.unlinked_pause`

> The rolls must have a brief pause between them.

### 27.9.3 {#rb-lines.length_equal}

`lines.length_equal`

> If any kind of roll is placed on an Interior Line, the lengths of the two parts of the line (Line Segments) before and after the roll must be equal.

### 27.9.4 {#rb-lines.length_penalty}

`lines.length_penalty`

> If within a figure, two or more Interior Lines, or Line Segments, must be of the same length, an observed variation is penalized by reducing the grade in the following manner: … a visible variation less than 2:1 - 1 point deduction; … variation from 2:1 but less than 3:1 - 2 point deduction; … variation of 3:1 or more - 3 point deduction;

### 27.9.5 {#rb-lines.length_basis}

`lines.length_basis`

> The basis for judging line length is the first Interior Line or Line Segment flown.

### 28.20.1 {#rb-rolls.rate}

`rolls.rate`

> Slow Rolls must be flown at a constant roll rate. If there is any variance in the roll rate, deduct one (1) point per variation.

### 28.20.2 {#rb-rolls.stop}

`rolls.stop`

> The rotation must end with a precise stop with the wings at the desired degree of rotation. If there is any over or under rotation, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees.

### 28.20.3 {#rb-rolls.path_horizontal}

`rolls.path_horizontal`

> When executing any aileron roll on horizontal and Looping Lines, the aircraft's CG trajectory must continue, during the rolling portion of the figure, to appear exactly the same as if there had there been no roll.

### 28.20.4 {#rb-rolls.path_vertical}

`rolls.path_vertical`

> When executing any aileron roll on 45 and vertical lines, the zero-lift axis must remain, during the rolling portion of the figure, at the same attitude to the flown line as if there had there been no roll.

### 28.21.3 {#rb-rolls.hesitation_rate}

`rolls.hesitation_rate`

> The rates of roll between each point must match. For each roll rate observed to be different from the first, deduct one (1) point.

### 28.21.4 {#rb-rolls.hesitation_pause}

`rolls.hesitation_pause`

> The duration of the pauses at each point must match. For each pause duration observed to be different from the first, deduct one (1) point.

### 28.22.1 {#rb-snap_rolls.definition}

`snap_rolls.definition`

> A snap roll is an Autorotation at a high angle of attack.

### 28.22.2 {#rb-snap_rolls.break}

`snap_rolls.break`

> The judge must see two things to determine that a positive snap roll has been correctly initiated: a) a rapid and clearly visible pitch rotation in the nose up / tail down sense. b) visible yaw rotation followed by Autorotation.

### 28.22.6 {#rb-snap_rolls.pre_roll}

`snap_rolls.pre_roll`

> If there is roll motion observed before the Autorotation starts, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees.

### 28.22.7 {#rb-snap_rolls.autorotation}

`snap_rolls.autorotation`

> Throughout the snap, the Autorotation must continue. If the Autorotation ceases before the end of the roll, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of rotation remaining.

### 28.22.8 {#rb-snap_rolls.exit}

`snap_rolls.exit`

> At the conclusion of the snap the aircraft must immediately adopt the attitude or flight path that conforms to the requirements of the underlying figure. If the original attitude or flight path angle is not reestablished, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees.

### 28.23.1 {#rb-snap_rolls.negative}

`snap_rolls.negative`

> For negative snap rolls, all criteria stated for positive snap rolls apply except in a negative snap roll the nose and tail of the aircraft must initially move in the nose down / tail up sense.

### 28.24.1 {#rb-spins.definition}

`spins.definition`

> A spin is an Autorotation performed on a steeply descending flight path following an aerodynamic stall. Spins only appear on vertical downlines.

### 28.24.2 {#rb-spins.entry}

`spins.entry`

> When the aircraft stalls, the aircraft must simultaneously move around all three flight axes: a) the nose will pitch toward the ground; b) the aircraft will yaw; and c) the aircraft will roll. For failure to achieve simultaneous motion about all three axes, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of deviation.

### 28.24.5 {#rb-spins.attitude}

`spins.attitude`

> During Autorotation, pitch angle and rotation rate may vary without penalty.

### 28.24.6 {#rb-spins.stop}

`spins.stop`

> After completion of the prescribed number of turns, the aircraft must stop rotating precisely on either the X or Y axis and in the direction of flight appropriate to the sequence being flown. If the aircraft does not end up with the correct alignment, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of error.

### 28.24.7 {#rb-spins.continue}

`spins.continue`

> Autorotation must continue throughout the spin. If the Autorotation ceases before the end of the spin, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of rotation remaining.

### 28.24.8 {#rb-spins.downline}

`spins.downline`

> A vertical downline must be established at the same time as, or shortly after, the cessation of autorotation.

### 28.4.2 {#rb-turns.rate}

`turns.rate`

> There must be a constant rate of turn. Deduct for each variation.

### 28.4.5 {#rb-turns.altitude}

`turns.altitude`

> The altitude must be constant. If the altitude changes, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees or 100 feet.

### 28.5.1 {#rb-turns.entry_bank}

`turns.entry_bank`

> In aerobatic competition, a turn is divided into three distinct phases: a) establishing a bank of at least 60° while maintaining the initial heading;

### 28.5.3 {#rb-turns.bank}

`turns.bank`

> If there is any change to the established angle of bank, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees.

### 28.6.4 {#rb-turns.rolling}

`turns.rolling`

> While the judge may expect the aircraft to be upright or inverted at certain points in the turn, the downgrades for these figures are based only on changes to rate of roll, rate of turn, and altitude.

### 28.6.5 {#rb-turns.rolling_rate}

`turns.rolling_rate`

> There must be a constant rate of roll. Deduct for each variation.

### 28.6.6 {#rb-turns.rolling_stop}

`turns.rolling_stop`

> The rate of roll must not stop (aside from any brief pause when changing roll directions). Deduct for each stop.

### 28.8.1 {#rb-stall_turns.definition}

`stall_turns.definition`

> A hammerhead is a 180 degree yaw rotation, in either direction, at the top of a vertical line.

### 28.8.3 {#rb-stall_turns.pivot}

`stall_turns.pivot`

> The pivot begins when the aircraft starts to yaw or when it starts to backslide prior to yaw. The pivot ends when the aircraft is established on the downline. During the pivot, the aircraft's CG may displace by up to one-half wingspan without penalty. The penalty for any additional displacement, either laterally or vertically, is one point per half wingspan.

### 28.8.4 {#rb-stall_turns.pivot_motion}

`stall_turns.pivot_motion`

> If there is any rolling or pitching motion during the pivot, deduct one (1) point for every five (5) degrees.

### 28.8.5 {#rb-stall_turns.wind_drift}

`stall_turns.wind_drift`

> During the pivot, there is no deduction for any CG lateral motion caused by wind drift.

### 28.9.1 {#rb-tailslides.definition}

`tailslides.definition`

> In a tailslide, the aircraft climbs vertically, stops, and slides backwards vertically before pivoting on the pitch axis to recover in a vertical down line.

### 28.9.1 {#rb-tailslides.lean}

`tailslides.lean`

> Leaning into the slide to better control the pivot direction is common practice. Regardless, the standard deduction of one (1) point for every five (5) degrees of deviation applies.

### 28.9.3 {#rb-tailslides.slide}

`tailslides.slide`

> The backwards slide begins when the aircraft ceases upward motion. The aircraft must slide backwards at least one-half of the fuselage length. If it fails to do so, mark the figure HZ.

### 28.9.4 {#rb-tailslides.recovery}

`tailslides.recovery`

> Following the backwards slide, the aircraft must then pivot in the correct direction to a vertical down position.

### 7.1.1 {#rb-box.limits}

`box.limits`

> Performances occur above a clearly marked area of 1,000 meters (approximately 3,280 feet) square whose central point is the intersection of the X and Y axes.
